Open source · GitHub Actions

items.title: STAX Framework
items.text:
A modern open-source opinionated GitHub Workflow Framework to combine and deploy all of your cloud infrastructure and services.

Developed by GEBIT Solutions.

Get started → Explore supported technologies →

items.title: Backends
items.text: stax owns the Terraform/OpenTofu backend type: the pipeline writes an override file with an azurerm backend for cloud: azure, an s3 backend for cloud: aws, or a local backend for stacks with local_backend: true. Keep an empty backend "s3" {} (or backend "azurerm" {}) block in the stack, or none at all; the bucket, key, region and flags come from the deployment context.

items.title: AWS S3
items.text: For cloud: aws the state lives in state_bucket_name in state_region, one key per stack. State is locked with S3 native locking (use_lockfile), which needs OpenTofu 1.10 or Terraform 1.11 or later. Create the bucket with the setup-state workflow (cloud: aws); it enables versioning, default encryption, a public access block, a TLS-only bucket policy and managed tags. Pass dry_run: true to only check the bucket and list what would change.

items.title: S3-compatible storage
items.text:
The S3 backend also works with S3-compatible stores such as Wasabi or MinIO. Point stax at the store with the optional deployment fields (or their GitHub variables):

deployment:
  cloud: aws
  default_location: eu-central-2
  state_region: eu-central-2
  state_bucket_name: example-tfstate
  aws_endpoint_url_s3: https://s3.eu-central-2.wasabisys.com
  aws_endpoint_url_sts: https://sts.wasabisys.com
  aws_endpoint_url_iam: https://iam.wasabisys.com
  aws_s3_compatible: true
  state_use_lockfile: false   # only until the store is known to support conditional writes
Field Effect aws_endpoint_url, aws_endpoint_url_s3, aws_endpoint_url_sts, aws_endpoint_url_iam Exported as AWS_ENDPOINT_URL, AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3, … to the init, plan, apply and output steps and the STS identity check. The S3 backend, the AWS provider and the AWS CLI read them. Other job steps, such as the SSM keystore, keep using AWS. aws_s3_compatible: true Sets AWS_REQUEST_CHECKSUM_CALCULATION and AWS_RESPONSE_CHECKSUM_VALIDATION to when_required for those steps and adds skip_s3_checksum, skip_region_validation and skip_requesting_account_id to the backend. aws_skip_sts_check: true Skips aws sts get-caller-identity and adds skip_credentials_validation to the backend. Use it for stores without an STS endpoint. state_use_lockfile: false Turns off S3 native locking for stores that do not support conditional writes. Nothing stops two runs of a stack from writing the state at the same time, so serialize deployments yourself. state_use_path_style: true Uses path-style addressing (https://host/bucket/key), which MinIO usually needs.

Notes:

  • Authenticate with the static AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY secrets. GitHub OIDC exchanges its token at AWS STS, so OIDC_ENABLED cannot be combined with aws_endpoint_url or aws_endpoint_url_sts.
  • The provider in your stack still needs settings that the backend flags do not cover, for example skip_region_validation and skip_requesting_account_id in the aws provider block for non-AWS regions.
  • For the state bucket, call the setup-state workflow with the same endpoints and aws_s3_compatible: "true". Versioning is required; public access block, default encryption, the TLS-only policy and tagging only warn when the store does not support them.

items.title: State configs
items.text:
STAX can also create the backend from a state config: a deploy config that contains only a deployment mapping with the backend coordinates. It must not define stacks.

# configs/state/dev.yaml: storage account only
deployment:
  cloud: azure
  default_location: northeurope
  state_resource_group_name: rg-shop-dev-tfstate
  state_storage_account_name: stshopdevstate

# configs/state/dev/shop.yaml: the same account plus the shop project's container
deployment:
  cloud: azure
  default_location: northeurope
  state_resource_group_name: rg-shop-dev-tfstate
  state_storage_account_name: stshopdevstate
  state_container_name: shop-tfstate

# configs/state/aws.yaml
deployment:
  cloud: aws
  default_location: eu-central-1   # region fallback when state_region is empty
  state_bucket_name: example-shop-tfstate
Field Azure AWS cloud Required Required default_location Required: location of new resources Region fallback state_resource_group_name Required Not used state_storage_account_name Required, 3-24 lowercase letters or digits after normalization Not used state_container_name Optional: omit it to deploy the account only Not used state_bucket_name Not used Required state_region Not used Optional aws_endpoint_url, aws_endpoint_url_s3, aws_endpoint_url_sts, aws_s3_compatible, aws_skip_sts_check Not used Optional: S3-compatible stores, as above

Empty fields fall back to the GitHub variables listed in Configuration. A run deploys one backend: when you select several files, later files override earlier values instead of adding containers. To share one storage account between projects, give each project its own config with the same account and its own state_container_name, and run the workflow once per config.

items.title: Deploy workflow
items.text:
Call a-wf-setup-ci.yml with config-profile: state, then pass its outputs to a-wf-deploy-state.yml. The repository that calls the workflows owns the configs, the GitHub Environment and the cloud credentials.

# .github/workflows/state.yml
name: "Deploy: state backend"

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      environment:
        description: GitHub Environment with the cloud credentials
        required: true
        type: environment
      state-config:
        description: State config under configs/state/, without .yaml
        required: true
        type: string
      dry-run:
        description: Plan only
        type: boolean
        default: true

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write

jobs:
  setup:
    uses: GEBITSolutions/stax/.github/workflows/a-wf-setup-ci.yml@<ref>
    secrets: inherit
    with:
      environment: ${{ inputs.environment }}
      stack_filter: ""
      config-profile: state
      release_config_filepath: configs/state/${{ inputs.state-config }}.yaml
      dry-run: ${{ inputs.dry-run }}
      actions-version: <ref>

  state:
    needs: setup
    uses: GEBITSolutions/stax/.github/workflows/a-wf-deploy-state.yml@<ref>
    secrets: inherit
    with:
      env: ${{ needs.setup.outputs.env }}
      default_location: ${{ needs.setup.outputs.default-location }}
      actions-version: <ref>

Use the same <ref> for both workflows and both actions-version inputs.

With dry-run: true (the setup default), the plan job validates the config and writes the backend to the run summary; nothing is deployed and no cloud login happens. Set dry-run: false to deploy. destroy: true fails: state backends are never removed by STAX.

The workflow outputs the resolved backend (cloud, dry-run, resource-group-name, storage-account-name, container-name, location, bucket-name, region).

items.title: What gets deployed
items.text:
The provisioning job runs in the caller's GitHub Environment and logs in with its ARM_* variables (Azure) or AWS_* settings (AWS), using OIDC when OIDC_ENABLED is true. It is safe to run again: existing resources are reused and their security settings reapplied.

Azure

  • The resource group, if it does not exist, in default_location.
  • The storage account (Standard LRS, TLS 1.2, anonymous blob access disabled). The run fails if an account with that name exists in another resource group.
  • Blob versioning, change feed and seven-day soft delete.
  • The container, private, when state_container_name is set.

The identity needs Contributor on the subscription: the workflow creates the resource group and looks up the account name across the subscription. Containers are created with the account key; give the identities of your stack deployments Storage Blob Data Contributor on their container.

AWS

  • The S3 bucket, hardened as described in AWS S3. The config's AWS endpoint options are passed on, so S3-compatible stores work the same way.

items.title: Without a config
items.text: a-wf-setup-state.yaml provisions a backend from explicit inputs (resource_group_name, storage_account_name, container_name, create-container, location, bucket_name, region and the AWS endpoint options) and the TF_STATE_* variables. a-wf-deploy-state.yml calls it after resolving the config.

items.title: Deployment context
items.text:
Put deployment values under the top-level deployment mapping in configs/<name>.yaml, or set them as GitHub variables. The setup workflow reads this mapping to build the deployment environment. stax init lists every required value, each next to its GitHub variable, in one commented deployment block of configs/default.yaml. stax init --project shop additionally writes deployment.project: shop live.

# configs/default.yaml
deployment:
  project: shop
  customer_id: default
  stage: dev
  cloud: azure
  default_location: northeurope
  public_cloud_flag: true
  resource_group_name: rg-shop-dev
  dns_zone_name: example.com
  dns_zone_resource_group_name: rg-dns
  state_storage_account_name: shopstate
  state_container_name: shop-tfstate
  state_resource_group_name: rg-state
stacks: []

# configs/prod.yaml
deployment:
  stage: prod
  resource_group_name: rg-shop-prod
  state_container_name: shop-prod-tfstate
stacks: []

Selecting configs/prod.yaml uses its stage, resource group and state container. Supply the remaining required values through GitHub variables or add them to that selected YAML. A config without stacks deploys nothing; the CLI's validate config --strict reports it.

The setup workflow reads only the files you select. configs/default.yaml is a normal config file: it contributes no values when you select prod. The same rule applies to external configuration repositories.

For multiple configs, pass release_config_filepath: configs/prod.yaml,configs/region.yaml to the setup reusable workflow. Later selected files override earlier values in the shared run context. The generated Deploy form selects one config by name.

Precedence per field is selected YAML → GitHub variable. An empty string or null falls through to the GitHub variable if no other selected file supplies the field; false remains an explicit value.

items.title: Supported fields and GitHub variable fallback
items.text:
YAML deployment field GitHub variable Requirement project PROJECT (vars.project also works) Required customer_id CUSTOMER_ID Required stage STAGE Required cloud CLOUD Required; azure or aws default_location DEFAULT_LOCATION Required public_cloud_flag PUBLIC_CLOUD_FLAG Required; boolean true/false or their string forms resource_group_name RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME Required for Azure dns_zone_name DNS_ZONE_NAME Required for Azure dns_zone_resource_group_name DNS_ZONE_RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME Required for Azure state_storage_account_name STATE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT_NAME Required for Azure state_container_name STATE_CONTAINER_NAME Required for Azure state_resource_group_name STATE_RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME Required for Azure state_bucket_name STATE_BUCKET_NAME Required for AWS state_region STATE_REGION Required for AWS aws_endpoint_url AWS_ENDPOINT_URL Optional, AWS only; base endpoint for every AWS service aws_endpoint_url_s3 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3 Optional, AWS only; S3 endpoint for the state backend and the AWS provider aws_endpoint_url_sts AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_STS Optional, AWS only; not supported with OIDC_ENABLED aws_endpoint_url_iam AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_IAM Optional, AWS only aws_s3_compatible AWS_S3_COMPATIBLE Optional, AWS only; boolean, default false aws_skip_sts_check AWS_SKIP_STS_CHECK Optional, AWS only; boolean, default false state_use_lockfile STATE_USE_LOCKFILE Optional, AWS only; boolean, default true state_use_path_style STATE_USE_PATH_STYLE Optional, AWS only; boolean, default false

The optional AWS fields target S3-compatible storage such as Wasabi or MinIO; see Backends. Endpoint URLs must use https (http only for localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1]) and cannot contain credentials, query strings, fragments, whitespace or backslashes. Setting one of them to a non-default value with another cloud fails the setup.

These requirements apply to stack deployments. A state config, resolved with config-profile: state, needs only the backend fields; see Backends.

items.title: Stack conditions
items.text: A stack's if string is evaluated whether or not a stack filter is supplied. For example, if: "'{stage}' === 'prod'" selects the stack only for the production stage. A false condition excludes the stack; if every selected stack is excluded, the deployment plan is empty.

items.title: Installation
items.text: Use the STAX CLI to create a deployment workflow, add stacks and validate your configuration. You run the CLI locally; GitHub Actions runs your deployments.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• Node.js 24 or later, with npm.
  • A GitHub repository with GitHub Actions enabled.

Check your local installation:

node --version
npm --version

You do not need cloud credentials to install the CLI or generate project files. Configure credentials and deployment settings before running a deployment.

items.title: Choose an installation method
items.text: Use a project-local installation to share a locked CLI version with your team. Use a global installation to run stax across repositories without adding a dependency to each project. Prefer project-local installation when dealing with multiple projects to avoid version conflicts.

items.title: Project-local installation
items.text:
From the root of your project repository, install the CLI as a development dependency:

npm install --save-dev --save-exact @gebit/stax-cli

If your repository has no package.json yet, create one with npm init -y first.

npm saves the current release as an exact development dependency in your package.json. Add a stax entry to its scripts section, keeping your existing scripts and dependencies:

{
  "scripts": {
    "stax": "stax"
  }
}

Check that you can run the installed CLI:

npm run stax -- --help

Commit package.json and package-lock.json. Add node_modules/ to .gitignore. After cloning the repository, team members install the locked dependencies with:

npm ci

Use npm run stax -- <command> for this installation. npm uses the project's installed CLI; you do not need a global installation.

items.title: Global installation
items.text:
Install the CLI for use across repositories:

npm install --global @gebit/stax-cli

Check that the command is available:

stax --help

Use stax <command> for this installation.

items.title: Initialize your repository
items.text:
From the root of your project repository, run the command for your installation method:

Action Project-local Global Initialize the repository npm run stax -- init stax init Add a stack npm run stax -- add stax add Validate configuration npm run stax -- validate config stax validate config

Both installation methods use the installed CLI version when init writes the reusable workflow refs, actions-version inputs and editor schema URL. Choose a CLI release that matches the framework version you deploy. Existing workflows and configs do not update when you install a different CLI version.

The init command creates two files:

File Purpose .github/workflows/deploy.yml A manually triggered Deploy workflow that calls the STAX reusable workflows. configs/default.yaml An empty stack list, deployment-setting examples and a schema link for editor completion.

If you build the CLI from source (0.0.0-development), pass --framework-ref <tag-or-commit-sha> to init, for example stax init --framework-ref main. You can name a branch, including main, if you want that ref. Development builds have no default framework ref; published releases reject the override and use their installed version.

You can also set a project name and preselect a GitHub Environment during initialization:

# Project-local installation
npm run stax -- init --project my-project --environment dev

# Global installation
stax init --project my-project --environment dev

Use lowercase letters, digits and hyphens for the project name, starting with a letter. Create the GitHub Environment in your repository settings before deploying; --environment only sets the workflow form's default.

STAX leaves existing files unchanged unless you pass --force. Review those files before replacing them.

items.title: Check your configuration
items.text:
Run the validation command for your installation method from the table above. The initial configuration contains no stacks, so the validator reports a warning.

Local validation checks the configuration structure; it does not verify cloud access or guarantee that a deployment will succeed. The CLI allows deployment fields to remain unset because GitHub variables can supply them at runtime.

stax add and stax validate config use the schema bundled with the installed CLI and work offline. They do not fetch the editor schema URL in configs/default.yaml.

stax init does not deploy anything. Before running the generated workflow, add a stack and supply the required deployment settings and credentials. See Configuration for deployment fields and their matching GitHub variables.

items.title: Next step
items.text: Continue with Your first config to add a stack and configure your deployment.

items.title: Passing values between stacks
items.text: Stacks rarely stand alone. A cluster needs the network it runs in, and an application needs the address of its database. STAX lets one stack hand values to another: the first stack publishes outputs, and the second one reads them as inputs.

items.title: Inputs
items.text:
A stack lists the values it needs under input. Each entry gives the input a name and says where its value comes from:

stacks:
  - id: app
    type: opentofu
    folder: app
    input:
      - replicas: "2"                                             # a fixed value
      - resource_group: global.pipeline.var.resource_group_name   # a value of this deployment
      - app_name: global.config.var.app_name                      # a shared value from this config file
      - subnet_id: stack.network.var.subnet_id                    # an output of the network stack
      - global.pipeline.var.stage                                 # named after its last part: stage

The input name is what the stack sees: a Terraform or OpenTofu variable, or a shell variable in a script stack. When an entry is only a reference, without a name, the input takes the name of the reference's last part.

items.title: Where values can come from
items.text:
Reference Value global.pipeline.var.<name> A value of the current deployment, such as project, stage, customer_id, environment, cloud, resource_group_name, dry_run or release_tag_name. global.config.var.<name> A shared value from the top-level globals section of the same config file. stack.<id>.var.<name> An output of another stack. stack.<id>.secret.<name> An output of another stack that was stored as a secret. gh.var.<NAME> A variable of the GitHub Environment. gh.secret.<NAME> A secret of the GitHub Environment.

Anything that is not a reference is passed on as written.

Shared values belong to the file that defines them. Use them for names or settings that several stacks of one config repeat:

globals:
  app_name: shop

stacks:
  - id: frontend
    type: script
    script: scripts/frontend.sh
    input:
      - global.config.var.app_name

items.title: When a value is missing
items.text: If a referenced value does not exist, the stack fails and the log names the missing reference. A typo therefore stops the run instead of deploying a wrong value. The only exception is a destroy run of Terraform, OpenTofu and Azure Static Web Apps stacks, where a placeholder stands in so that removal is not blocked by values that are already gone.

items.title: Terraform and OpenTofu
items.text:
You do not have to declare anything to make an output available to stacks in the same config. When another stack reads stack.network.var.subnet_id, STAX publishes the subnet_id output of network automatically:

# network/outputs.tf
output "subnet_id" {
  value = azurerm_subnet.main.id
}

To publish an output that no stack in the config reads yet, for example for a separate config, list it under output-var, or under output-secret to store it as a secret:

  - id: network
    type: opentofu
    folder: network
    output-var: [subnet_id, vnet_name]
    output-secret: [admin_password]

items.title: Script stacks
items.text:
A script publishes values by writing two lines to $GITHUB_OUTPUT: output_vars and output_secrets, each a JSON object. Each name starts with the stack id in capital letters, hyphens replaced by underscores, followed by two underscores:

# Publishes "endpoint" for the stack with id "api".
prefix="$(tr '[:lower:]-' '[:upper:]_' <<<"${stack_id}")__"
{
  echo "output_vars=$(jq -nc --arg key "${prefix}ENDPOINT" --arg value "https://api.example.com" '{($key): $value}')"
  echo "output_secrets={}"
} >>"${GITHUB_OUTPUT}"

Another stack then reads it as stack.api.var.endpoint.

items.title: Reading a value also sets the order
items.text:
When a stack reads another stack's output, it automatically depends on that stack. You do not need to repeat it under depends_on:

stacks:
  - id: network
    type: opentofu
    folder: network

  - id: app
    type: opentofu
    folder: app
    input:
      - subnet_id: stack.network.var.subnet_id   # app now runs after network

If the referenced stack is not part of the selected config, STAX adds no dependency and logs a warning. The value is then read from what an earlier deployment stored, which is how one config can use outputs of another.

items.title: Where outputs are stored
items.text:
Outputs are stored per GitHub Environment, so dev and prod keep separate values. Configure one store per environment; STAX reads from the first one it finds in this order:

Store Configure with AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store Variable REPO_KEYSTORE_SSM_PREFIX Azure Key Vault Variable REPO_KEYSTORE_KEY_VAULT_URL GitHub Environment (default) A GitHub App with the variable RELEASE_APP_CLIENT_ID and the secret RELEASE_APP_CLIENT_SECRET, or a token in the secret CI_ENV_TRANSFER_GH_TOKEN

With the default store, an output appears as a variable or secret of the environment, for example NETWORK__SUBNET_ID. The GitHub App or token needs write access to the repository's environments, variables and secrets.

Outputs are only stored by real deployments. A dry run uses the values from the last real deployment. On the first dry run of a new config, a stack that reads another stack's output therefore fails until that stack has been deployed once.

items.title: Release notes
items.text:
STAX can write a plain-English release note for every pull request and keep it in the pull-request description, where authors can read and edit it. The reusable workflow a-wf-release-notes.yml runs on each push to a same-repository pull request and maintains a Release notes section at the end of the description:

  • a first line **Breaking change:** No or **Breaking change:** Yes. <what stops working or changes>. <what users must do>.;
  • one to seven short bullets, one line each, stating what changed for users (related changes grouped);
  • links back to the pull request and the issues it closes.

The section is replaced on every push. To keep a hand-edited version, put <!-- release-notes:keep --> on a line of its own inside the section.

items.title: Add it to a repository
items.text:
name: Release notes

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, ready_for_review]

permissions:
  contents: read
  issues: read
  pull-requests: write

concurrency:
  group: release-notes-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  release-notes:
    uses: GEBITSolutions/stax/.github/workflows/a-wf-release-notes.yml@<version>
    with:
      model: my-model
      actions-version: <version>
    secrets:
      llm-base-url: ${{ secrets.LLM_BASE_URL }}
      llm-api-key: ${{ secrets.LLM_API_KEY }}
Input or secret Required Purpose model yes Model or deployment name served by the endpoint. llm-base-url (secret) yes OpenAI Responses-compatible base URL ending in /v1, for example https://api.openai.com/v1. It is a secret so the endpoint stays out of public logs. llm-api-key (secret) yes Key for the endpoint, sent as a bearer token. instructions-path no Custom instructions on the caller's base branch. The default is .github/release-notes/instructions.md. release-app-client-id, release-app-private-key (secret) no GitHub App that edits the description; it needs the repository permission Pull requests: Read and write. Without it, the job token edits it as github-actions[bot]. environment no GitHub environment of the job (default release-notes); each run is listed under Deployments with a link to the pull request. Protection rules on it would hold the job. max-diff-chars no Diff characters passed to the agent (default 120000); longer diffs are truncated.

Fork and Dependabot pull requests are skipped because they receive no secrets; drafts are skipped until they are ready for review.

items.title: In releases
items.text:
When a-wf-release.yml or a-wf-release-prepare.yml prepares a release, it asks GitHub which pull request each first-parent commit since the previous release tag merged, and writes their sections into a ## Release <version> entry of CHANGELOG.md and into the release body: breaking changes first, then the changes, then pull requests merged without a note. The pre-release shows this draft, so it can be checked before the release is approved.

During the transition from JSON release notes, the next release also includes release-ready/release-notes/pr-*.json files and a hand-written ## Unreleased section of CHANGELOG.md.

items.title: Migrating from the Copilot workflow
items.text: a-wf-copilot-generate-release-notes.yml is deprecated and will be removed in the next major release. Replace its caller with the workflow shown above: drop the pr_number, branch and base_ref inputs and the COPILOT_USER_TOKEN secret, and pass model, llm-base-url and llm-api-key. Pending release-ready/release-notes/*.json files are still collected by the next release.

items.title: How the agent is isolated
items.text:
The note is written by Letta Code in a pinned container image, on the local backend and --ephemeral: no agent, memory or account is kept, and telemetry and auto-update are off. The agent receives the title, description, commits, diff and closed issues in its prompt and may additionally read the checkout. The workflow:

  • mounts the pull-request checkout read-only and deletes symlinks from it first;
  • allows only Read, Glob and Grep below the checkout, in strict permission mode, so every other tool call is denied;
  • starts the agent outside the checkout, so settings or skills in the pull request cannot widen its permissions;
  • runs the agent on an internal Docker network without DNS. Its only peer is a relay (pinned nginx) that forwards the endpoint's /v1/ route over verified TLS and adds the real key. The agent only holds a dummy key, and the job fails if the agent container can reach anything else.

Instructions, the relay configuration and scripts come from the STAX checkout selected by actions-repository and actions-version, not from the pull request. Custom instructions are read from the base branch.

items.title: Running a deployment
items.text: Every deployment starts from the Deploy workflow that stax init created. This page explains the choices on its form, what happens during a run, and how to read the result.

items.title: The Deploy form
items.text:
Open Actions → Deploy → Run workflow. The form has five fields:

Field What it does Environment The GitHub Environment to deploy to. Its variables, secrets and protection rules apply to the whole run. Stack filter Which stacks to deploy. Leave it empty to deploy every stack in the config. See Choosing stacks. Deploy config The file in configs/ to use, without .yaml. The default is default. Dry run On by default. Every stack plans or checks its changes without applying them. Destroy Removes what the selected stacks created instead of deploying them.

Start with a dry run whenever you change a config, and switch it off once the plan looks right.

items.title: What happens during a run
items.text:
A run has two parts.

Setup CI/CD prepares the deployment:

  1. It reads the selected config file.
  2. It combines the deployment values with the GitHub variables of the environment. Values in the config win.
  3. It checks that every required value and the cloud sign-in details are present, and stops with a clear message if something is missing.
  4. It works out the order of the stacks and writes an overview to the run summary.

Deploy Levels then deploys the stacks in that order.

items.title: How STAX orders stacks
items.text:
STAX groups your stacks into layers. A stack goes into a later layer than every stack it depends on. A stack depends on another one when it lists it under depends_on, or when it reads one of its values, as described in Passing values between stacks.

stacks:
  - id: network
    type: opentofu
    folder: network

  - id: cluster
    type: opentofu
    folder: cluster
    depends_on: [network]

  - id: dns
    type: opentofu
    folder: dns

Here network and dns form the first layer and run side by side. cluster waits for network and runs in the second layer.

Some rules to keep in mind:

  • Stacks in the same layer run in parallel. If one of them fails, the others still finish, but no later layer starts.
  • A config can have at most 14 layers.
  • A destroy run walks the layers backwards, so dependent stacks are removed before the stacks they rely on.
  • A stack whose if condition is false is left out, for example if: "'{stage}' === 'prod'" for a production-only stack. If every selected stack is left out, the run deploys nothing.

items.title: Choosing stacks
items.text:
The Stack filter field takes one or more entries, separated by commas:

Entry Selects cluster Only the stack with that id. >cluster The stack and everything it depends on, all the way down. network< The stack and the stacks that depend on it directly. group-core Every stack that lists group-core under stack-groups.

Group names must start with group-:

stacks:
  - id: network
    type: opentofu
    folder: network
    stack-groups: [group-core]

Filtering by id alone deploys only that stack. It does not deploy what the stack depends on, so make sure those stacks are already in place, or use >.

items.title: Dry runs
items.text:
A dry run goes through the same steps as a real deployment, up to the point where something would change:

  • Terraform and OpenTofu stacks create a plan and stop.
  • Script stacks still run, with DRY_RUN=true, so each script decides what to skip.
  • No stack stores its output values. A stack that reads another stack's value gets whatever the last real deployment stored.

Runs queue instead of overlapping: dry runs of the same commit share one queue, and real deployments to the same environment share another. A new run waits for the one in progress instead of cancelling it. If several runs are waiting in the same queue, GitHub keeps only the newest.

items.title: Approvals and protection
items.text: Every stack runs as its own job in the chosen GitHub Environment. Protection rules on that environment, such as required reviewers or allowed branches, therefore apply to the run. Protect production environments, and keep dry runs in mind: they use the same environment and its credentials.

items.title: Reading the result
items.text:
• The run summary shows the stacks of this run, their layers and how they depend on each other, together with the config file and the commit it was read from.
  • Each stack appears as its own job, named after the stack's name. Open it to see the plan, the script output or the error.
  • Failed setup steps name the missing value, variable or secret. Add it to the config or the environment and run again.

items.title: Supported stack types
items.text:
Combine these technologies and workflow types in your STAX Framework deployment stacks.

Checked boxes indicate support. Unchecked boxes indicate planned support, not available yet.

items.title: Infrastructure as code
items.text:
• Terraform (terraform): provision cloud infrastructure.
  • OpenTofu (opentofu): provision cloud infrastructure.
  • Bicep (bicep): provision Azure infrastructure.
  • CDK: planned, not supported yet.

items.title: Docker and image builds
items.text:
• Docker (docker-build-push): build container images and push them to a registry.
  • Packer (packer): build machine images for Azure Compute Gallery or Hetzner Cloud. AWS AMIs are reserved and not implemented.

items.title: Packer images
items.text:
type: packer takes packer_directory, an exact packer_version, and an optional packer_template (default .). build_target selects the publisher. Omit it, or set azure, to keep today's Azure Compute Gallery behavior.

The template owns the source block (builder, base image, provisioners) and must declare any Packer variables it reads. STAX owns credentials, the injected var-file, packer fmt / init / validate, publishing, retention, and outputs. A Hetzner template must write manifest.json with a manifest post-processor. Gallery builds still take image_id from az sig image-version show; the manifest is optional there.

Packer input conversion still comes from GEBITSolutions/stax at actions-version. The build-target helper is loaded from that same trusted checkout (.github/scripts/packer-build-target.mjs). actions-version has to include this change. dry_run remains the default, so a Hetzner build does not create a server unless dry-run is turned off. There is no extra environment protection rule.

STAX injects stax_build_target, stax_stack_id, stax_env, stax_git_sha and stax_image_version only when the template declares that variable, so existing Gallery templates keep validating. It also flattens azure.* or hetzner.* into the same .pkrvars.json file as stack inputs. An input that disagrees with the build-target field fails the run.

build_target Credentials Publish azure (default) ARM_* and OIDC_ENABLED, unchanged Compute Gallery image version. destroy is rejected. hetzner HCLOUD_TOKEN on the GitHub Environment Labelled snapshot. keep_last (default 3) deletes older matches. destroy: true deletes matches beyond keep_last, or all of them when keep_last is 0. aws Reserved Not implemented. stax validate config warns; the workflow fails. The output names will not change when an AMI executor is added.

azure fields are image_resource_group_name, gallery_name, image_definition_name, image_version and target_regions. The same names at the top level of the stack are deprecated aliases. Configs that still pass them through input do not need either form.

hetzner requires location and server_type (cax11 is arm64; the template's base image must match, STAX does not translate architecture). Optional: snapshot_name (default: the stack id), snapshot_labels, keep_last. STAX merges labels with stax_stack_id, stax_env, stax_git_sha, stax_build_target=hetzner and managed_by=stax, and those keys win. A cax11 build is about €0.01 per hour; snapshots are about €0.017 per GB-month. The job summary prints that estimate. dry_run validates the template and does not create a server or call the Hetzner API.

Downstream stacks read published values with stack.<id>.var.<output>:

Output Meaning image_id Gallery version resource ID, Hetzner snapshot id, or later an AMI id image_ref azure:gallery:<resource-group>/<gallery>/<definition>/<version> or hcloud:snapshot:<id> build_target azure, hetzner, or later aws version Gallery image_version, or 0.0.0+<git sha> for Hetzner labels JSON object of tags or snapshot labels git_sha Source commit

output-var lists which of those to export. A list that only contains image_id still exports only that value.

stacks:
  - id: golden-hetzner
    type: packer
    packer_directory: packer/base-image
    packer_template: .
    packer_version: "1.16.1"
    build_target: hetzner
    hetzner:
      location: fsn1
      server_type: cax11
      snapshot_name: base-image-golden
      snapshot_labels:
        base-image: "true"
        role: golden
      keep_last: 3
    output-var: [image_id, image_ref, build_target, version, labels]

items.title: Packages
items.text: • RPM (rpmbuild): build RPM packages.

items.title: Deployments
items.text:
• Cloud functions (function-build-deploy): build and deploy cloud functions.
  • Azure Static Web Apps (swa-site-deploy): deploy websites.
  • Azure Static Web Apps documentation (swa-docs-site-deploy): deploy documentation sites.
  • Amazon S3 (s3-site-deploy): deploy static websites.
  • GitHub Pages (github-pages-site-deploy): build MkDocs or Zensical documentation, or publish a prebuilt static site.

items.title: Scripts
items.text:
Use the script workflow type to run custom scripts:

  • Bash: run shell scripts.
  • Python: run Python scripts.

items.title: Helm deployments
items.text: • Helm: planned, not supported yet.

items.title: Raw Kubernetes manifest deployments
items.text: • Kubernetes manifests: planned, not supported yet.

items.title: Why STAX?
items.text:
Cloud engineering and DevOps teams solve many of the same CI/CD problems in every project: deploying infrastructure and services, generating releases, reviewing pull requests, running dry runs, and performing static code analysis. Rebuilding these workflows takes time. Keeping copied implementations in sync adds ongoing maintenance work.

Reusable GitHub Actions workflows and actions help reduce that duplication, but they still need project-specific integration. Teams must connect build and deployment steps, configure cloud authentication, manage access to external repositories, and coordinate the order in which components are deployed.

STAX aims to address these challenges by reducing repetitive setup and project-specific integration work. It goes beyond workflow reuse by letting teams describe infrastructure components and their relations in configuration files, making delivery easier to manage as projects grow.

items.title: Bring related components together
items.text:
A project rarely consists of a single deployment. It may combine infrastructure, container images, application builds, scripts, and Kubernetes deployments using manifests or Helm charts.

STAX organizes these units as stacks. The goal is to keep infrastructure provisioning and service delivery together, with a shared approach to configuration and orchestration across different technologies.

items.title: Make dependencies explicit
items.text:
Stacks often depend on one another. A cluster needs its network before it can be provisioned. A container deployment needs both a built image and a running target environment. Some stacks also need output values from earlier deployments, such as a resource identifier or service endpoint.

STAX aims to make these relationships explicit, so deployment order and the flow of values between stacks are part of the project configuration instead of custom coordination logic scattered across workflows.

items.title: Start new projects with less setup
items.text: A consistent framework reduces the decisions and repetitive work involved in getting a project started. STAX aims to help teams bootstrap new projects, reuse deployment patterns, and extend their configuration as new components are added.

items.title: Stay within GitHub
items.text:
STAX draws inspiration from Spacelift and Atmos, particularly their approaches to organizing infrastructure and coordinating stacks.

Its design goal is to provide that orchestration within GitHub Actions, without requiring a separate SaaS platform. Beyond GitHub and the services being deployed, a cloud storage service may be needed to hold values passed between stacks. This orchestration state is distinct from any infrastructure state managed by the underlying tools.

items.title: Your first config
items.text:
This guide takes you from an empty repository to a first deployment. You add one small script stack, try it with a dry run, then deploy it for real. A script stack is the simplest stack type, so you can see how STAX works before you add infrastructure.

You need a repository initialized with stax init, as described in Installation. The examples use the global stax command; with a project-local installation, run npm run stax -- <command> instead.

items.title: What stax init gave you
items.text:
stax init created two files:

  • .github/workflows/deploy.yml: the Deploy workflow you start from the GitHub Actions tab.
  • configs/default.yaml: your deploy config. It starts with an empty stack list and a commented deployment block that lists every value STAX needs.

A deploy config describes two things: the deployment (which project, stage and cloud you deploy to) and the stacks (the parts you deploy, in which order, and with which values).

items.title: Add a stack
items.text:
Create a small script in your repository:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/hello.sh
set -euo pipefail

# STAX passes the stack inputs as "export name=value" lines in the first argument.
eval "${1:-}"

echo "Hello from ${stack_id}: ${greeting}, stage ${stage}"

if [[ "${DRY_RUN}" == "true" ]]; then
  echo "Dry run: nothing changed"
  exit 0
fi

echo "This is where a real deployment would change something"

Then describe it as a stack in configs/default.yaml:

stacks:
  - id: hello
    name: Hello
    type: script
    script: scripts/hello.sh
    input:
      - greeting: hello
      - global.pipeline.var.stage

What each line means:

  • id identifies the stack. Other stacks use it to depend on this one or to read its values. Stick to lowercase letters, digits and hyphens: the id also becomes part of the names under which the stack's values are stored.
  • name is the label shown in the GitHub Actions run.
  • type: script runs a Bash script. The path in script is relative to your repository root.
  • input lists the values the stack receives. greeting: hello is a fixed value. global.pipeline.var.stage takes the stage of the current deployment, and the script receives it as stage.

STAX also gives every script its own stack id as stack_id and the DRY_RUN flag. Your script decides what a dry run means: STAX runs it either way.

Keep input values free of spaces and quotes for script stacks; they are passed to the script unquoted.

You can also add a stack interactively with stax add, which asks for the type and the required fields.

items.title: Fill in the deployment
items.text:
Before any stack runs, STAX checks the deployment values and your cloud sign-in details, even for a stack that never touches the cloud. Uncomment the deployment block in configs/default.yaml and fill it in, or set the same values as GitHub variables. A complete Azure example:

deployment:
  project: hello-stax
  customer_id: default
  stage: dev
  cloud: azure
  default_location: westeurope
  public_cloud_flag: true
  resource_group_name: rg-hello-dev
  dns_zone_name: example.com
  dns_zone_resource_group_name: rg-dns
  state_storage_account_name: sthellodevstate
  state_container_name: tfstate
  state_resource_group_name: rg-hello-state

Configuration lists every field, its GitHub variable, and which fields AWS needs instead.

items.title: Prepare the GitHub Environment
items.text:
Each deployment runs in a GitHub Environment, for example dev. Create it under Settings → Environments and add the sign-in details for your cloud:

Cloud Variables Secrets Azure ARM_CLIENT_ID, ARM_TENANT_ID, ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID ARM_CLIENT_SECRET, unless you sign in with OIDC (OIDC_ENABLED=true) AWS AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, or AWS_ROLE_ARN with OIDC (OIDC_ENABLED=true)

Values you prefer not to commit, such as the subscription or account details, can live here as variables instead of in the config.

Check the config locally before you push:

stax validate config

Validation checks the structure of your config. It cannot check your cloud access or the contents of the GitHub Environment; the first run does that.

items.title: Run a dry run
items.text:
Commit and push the config and the script. Then open Actions → Deploy → Run workflow and choose:

  • Environment: dev
  • Deploy config: default
  • Dry run: on (the default)

The run has two parts. Setup CI/CD reads your config, checks the deployment values and sign-in details, and works out the order of the stacks. Deploy Levels then runs the stacks. In the log of the Hello job you will see the greeting and "Dry run: nothing changed".

If setup fails, its message names the missing value or variable. Add it to the config or the GitHub Environment and run again.

items.title: Deploy
items.text:
Run the workflow again with Dry run switched off. The script now runs with DRY_RUN=false.

That is the whole loop: describe a stack, try it with a dry run, then deploy. A real project replaces the script with infrastructure, image builds or sites; see Supported stack types.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Running a deployment explains the Deploy form and how STAX orders and runs your stacks.
  • Passing values between stacks shows how one stack uses what another one created.
